title: How Body Armor Levels Actually Work

lines.text: This is every level of American body armor, from a vest that stops a pistol to a plate that stops an armor-piercing rifle round.
And one of the most popular levels you can buy does not officially exist.
Step one. Level Two A.
The thinnest armor on the list. A soft, flexible vest, made from layers of woven fiber.
It was tested against a nine millimeter bullet traveling at 1,225 feet per second.
And in the newest standard, it is gone. Level Two A was dropped completely.
Step two. Level Two.
Thicker, still soft, and rated for nine millimeter and .357 Magnum rounds.
Soft armor like this owes a lot to one man. In 1972, a pizza shop owner named Richard Davis knelt at a police range in Walled Lake, Michigan, and shot himself in the chest.
He was wearing his own vest. He stood up, and kept shooting at the targets.
He went on to repeat that demonstration more than 190 times.
In the new system, Level Two is called H G one. H G, for handgun.
Step three. Level Three A.
The strongest soft armor there is. It adds the .44 Magnum, one of the most powerful handgun rounds made.
It is still something you can wear under a shirt. It is now called H G two.
And no soft vest on this list will stop a rifle.
Step four is not a level at all. It is the rule that decides every level.
Stopping the bullet is not enough. Behind the armor, testers place a block of clay.
When the bullet hits, the armor bends, and pushes a dent into that clay.
If the dent is deeper than 44 millimeters, about an inch and three quarters, the armor fails, even if the bullet never got through.
Step five. Level Three.
This is where soft armor ends. Level Three is a rigid plate, made of ceramic, steel or polyethylene.
Its test round is the 7.62 NATO rifle bullet, at 2,780 feet per second. More than twice as fast as the Level Two A test.
The plate has to stop six of them.
Its new name is R F one. R F, for rifle.
Step six. Level Three plus.
You will find it on armor websites everywhere. It is the level people argue about most.
And it was never an official level. There is no Level Three plus in the government standard.
Makers invented it to say their plates stop more than Level Three, usually the green-tipped 5.56 round. But what plus means changes from one company to the next.
Step seven. R F two.
So the newest standard did something about it. It created a brand new level between Three and Four.
R F two must stop everything R F one does, plus the green-tipped 5.56 round. The gap that marketing filled now has a real name.
Step eight. Level Four.
The top of the ladder. Its test round is the .30-06 armor-piercing bullet, with a hardened steel core.
It is now called R F three.
So here is the whole ladder. Two A is gone. Two is H G one. Three A is H G two. Three is R F one. Three plus became R F two. And Four is R F three.
The level that does not exist was so popular that the government finally had to make it real.
Which level would you trust with your life? Tell me in the comments.
